stem: Below are 8 rhythm strips. Match the rhythm strip or ECG to the correct diagnosis:

items.right: Third degree AV block (complete heart block)

answer:
The pairings:

Rhythm stripDiagnosis
Strip APremature atrial contraction
Strip BFirst degree AV block
Strip CSecond degree AV block
Strip DThird degree AV block (complete heart block)
Strip EVentricular fibrillation
Strip FAtrial flutter
Strip GPremature ventricular contraction(s)

From 02 - Bradycardia and 04 - Tachycardia. Each one has its own discriminator:

  • A, PAC: an early narrow beat with an abnormal P, then a pause.
  • B, 1st degree AV block: PR > 200 ms with every P conducted.
  • C, 2nd degree AV block: some P waves without a QRS, so beats come in groups.
  • D, 3rd degree block: AV dissociation. P waves march through a slow, regular, wide ventricular escape.
  • E, VF: chaotic baseline, no organised QRS.
  • F, atrial flutter: continuous sawtooth flutter waves between narrow QRSs.
  • G, PVCs: early, wide, bizarre QRSs with no preceding P.

The stem says 8 strips, but only 7 are shown and 7 are listed.
note: answer key A-i ... G-vii (strip letters are the figure's labels)

stem: Match the coronary artery to the location of infarction
answer:
The pairings:

Coronary arteryLocation of infarction
Left Anterior Descending ArteryAnterior MI
Right Coronary ArteryInferior MI
Left Circumflex ArteryPosterior MI

From 04 - Myocardial Infarction. The culprit artery sets the wall that infarcts:

  • LAD - anterior MI: ST elevation in the anterior leads V3-V4 (V1-V6 if it extends septal and lateral). The LAD supplies the anterior wall and the anterior two-thirds of the septum.
  • RCA - inferior MI: ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal depression in I and aVL. In the 85% who are right-dominant, the RCA gives the posterior descending artery.
  • Left circumflex - posterior MI: often missed on a 12-lead. Look for ST depression in V1-V3 or add V8-V9.

answer:

From 01 - Anatomy of the Neck. The key reads: label A = sternocleidomastoid, B = trapezius, C = middle scalene, D = anterior scalene. Use their relationships to place each one:

  • Sternocleidomastoid: the large diagonal muscle that divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles. Most of the neck's nerves lie deep to it.
  • Trapezius: the back edge of the posterior triangle, running out to the scapula.
  • Anterior scalene: in the floor of the posterior triangle, with the phrenic nerve on its anterior surface.
  • Middle scalene: just posterior to it, flexing the neck laterally. The brachial plexus emerges between the two scalenes.

stem: Typically, neural structures run with vascular structures. Match common pairings that we see running adjacent to one another in the neck.
answer:
The pairings:

NerveArtery it runs with
Hypoglossal nerveLingual artery
Vagus nerveCommon carotid artery
Superior laryngeal nerveSuperior thyroid artery

From 01 - Anatomy of the Neck. Each nerve runs with the vessel serving the same territory:

  • Vagus nerve with the common carotid artery: both lie in the carotid sheath, with the vagus between the internal jugular vein and the carotid.
  • Superior laryngeal nerve with the superior thyroid artery: the first branch of the external carotid runs down to the larynx and thyroid beside the nerve's external branch. That is why ligating the artery at thyroidectomy can injure the nerve, giving a weak, tired voice from cricothyroid palsy.

stem: Match the correct structure to each relationship term to describe the relationship of the esophagus to each structure. The esophagus is {relationship} to {structure}:
answer:
The pairings:

StructureThe esophagus is ... to it
TracheaPosterior
Thoracic aortaAnterolateral (right)
Azygous veinsAnterior

The esophagus passes through thoracic inlet posterior to the trachea. It runs anterolateral to the thoracic aorta on the right hand side, passes through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm into the abdominal cavity at the level of the T10 vertebra. The left bronchus and aortic arch pass anterior to the esophagus. On the right, the esophagus is covered by mediastinal pleura and anteriorly it is separated from the left atrium by the pericardium. The esophagus lies anterior to the thoracic duct and the azygos and hemiazygos veins.

stem: Match the expected manometric findings to the disorder:
answer:
The pairings:

Manometric findingDisorder
Aperistalsis + impaired LES relaxationAchalasia
Aperistalsis + hypotensive LESScleroderma
Simultaneous premature contractionsDistal esophageal spasm
High amplitude repetitive contractionsJackhammer esophagus
Weak amplitude slowly propagating contractionsNone of the listed disorders

From 04 - Esophageal Dysphagia. Motility disorders are diagnosed by manometry, not endoscopy. Each pattern pairs peristalsis with how the LES behaves:

  • Achalasia = aperistalsis + impaired LES relaxation: the LES fails to relax, giving a bird's-beak on barium swallow.
  • Scleroderma = aperistalsis + hypotensive LES: scarring weakens both, so reflux, strictures and Barrett's follow.
  • Distal esophageal spasm = simultaneous premature contractions, which are non-propulsive.
  • Jackhammer = high-amplitude repetitive contractions.
  • None = weak, slowly propagating contractions, which match none of the four.

The LES separates the two aperistaltic disorders: it is tight in achalasia and slack in scleroderma.
note: answer key A-I ... E-V

stem: Match the appropriate cause of hypoxemia to the clinical description:

items.left: Large mucous plug completely occluding the left mainstem bronchus
Reduced minute ventilation due to narcotics
Interstitial fibrosis in a patient with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

answer:
The pairings:

Clinical descriptionCause of hypoxemia
Large mucous plug completely occluding the left mainstem bronchusShunt
Acute pulmonary embolismV/Q mismatch
Reduced minute ventilation due to narcoticsHypoventilation
Interstitial fibrosis in a patient with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosisDiffusion impairment

From 02 - Gas Exchange and Hypoxia and the V/Q section of 03 - Lung Physiology - Ventilation. Map each lesion to what it does to ventilation, perfusion or the barrier:

  • Occluding mucous plug – shunt: a plug completely occluding a mainstem bronchus leaves perfused lung with no ventilation (V/Q = 0). The lecture's partial mucous plugs only lower V/Q; total occlusion is a true shunt that 100% O2 will not correct.
  • Pulmonary embolism – V/Q mismatch: PE leaves lung ventilated but not perfused, i.e. dead space (V/Q → ∞).
  • Narcotics – hypoventilation: narcotics suppress respiratory drive; PaCO2 rises and the A–a gradient stays normal.
  • Interstitial fibrosis – diffusion impairment: fibrosis thickens the blood–gas barrier (Fick's law), with ↓ DLCO.
note: answer key A-ii, B-i, C-iii, D-iv

stem: Match the muscle of the larynx with its function.
answer:
The pairings:

MuscleFunction
Cricothyroid muscleLengthens the vocal cords
Vocalis muscleShortens the vocal cords
Posterior cricoarytenoid muscleAbducts the vocal cords
Lateral cricoarytenoid musclePivot-adducts the vocal cords
Interarytenoid muscleTranslational-adducts the vocal cords
Aryepiglottic musclePulls epiglottis down

From 05 - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory System. Each muscle acts on either the cricothyroid joint (pitch) or the cricoarytenoid joint (opening and closing):

  • Cricothyroid: cricothyroid tilts the cricothyroid joint to lengthen the cords (↑ pitch). It is the only one supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
  • Vocalis: vocalis/thyroarytenoid shorten the cords (↓ pitch).
  • Posterior cricoarytenoid: posterior cricoarytenoid rotates the vocal processes laterally. It is the only abductor.
  • Lateral cricoarytenoid: lateral cricoarytenoid rotates them medially, a pivot adduction.
  • Interarytenoid: interarytenoid slides the arytenoids together, a translational adduction synergistic with the lateral cricoarytenoid.
  • Aryepiglottic: aryepiglottic pulls the epiglottis down to close the inlet in swallowing.
note: answer key A-iv, B-v, C-iii, D-ii, E-i, F-vi

stem: Match the correct structure to the number on the diagram below.
answer:
The pairings:

Number on diagramStructure
Label 1Mouth
Label 2Esophagus
Label 3Liver
Label 4Gall bladder
Label 5Duodenum
Label 6Ascending colon
Label 7Cecum
Label 8Descending colon
Label 9Rectum
Label 10Stomach

From 01 - Overview of the GI Tract. Follow food down the tract: mouth (1), where mechanical digestion and salivary starch digestion begin; esophagus (2), between the UES and LES; stomach (10), the main site of digestion, behind the pyloric sphincter; then duodenum (5), the first part of the small intestine. The accessory organs sit in the right upper quadrant: liver (3) with the gallbladder (4) tucked beneath it. The colon then runs from the cecum (7) in the right lower quadrant, past the ileocecal sphincter, up as the ascending colon (6), down the left as the descending colon (8), and ends at the rectum (9) before the anal sphincters.

Chewing, mixing of food and initial digestion of starch
Churning, production and secretion of gastric juice (acid), initial digestion of proteins
Absorption of water and electrolytes, formation and storage of feces until defecation

answer:

GI tract componentMain function

From 01 - Overview of the GI Tract and 10 - GI Secretion. Each organ's job follows from what it adds or removes:

  • Salivary glands = saliva with water, electrolytes, mucus and enzymes: the secretion itself.
  • Mouth and esophagus = chewing, mixing and initial starch digestion: salivary amylase acts during chewing.
  • Stomach = churning, acid secretion and initial protein digestion: HCl plus pepsin.
  • Small intestine = absorption of nutrients and water, and digestion: villi and microvilli make it the main absorptive site.
  • Large intestine = water and electrolyte absorption, and forming and storing feces.
  • Liver and gallbladder = producing and storing bile.
  • Pancreas = enzymes and bicarbonate: bicarbonate neutralises acidic chyme.

stem: Match the GI hormone or molecule with its corresponding function in the GI tract:

items.right: Stimulates motility, secretion and mediates nociception in the GI tract

answer:
The pairings:

Hormone or moleculeFunction
GastrinStimulates gastric acid secretion
SerotoninStimulates motility, secretion and mediates nociception in the GI tract
CCKInhibits gastric emptying

From 01 - Overview of the GI Tract and 10 - GI Secretion. Match each molecule by its signature action:

  • Serotonin = stimulates motility and secretion, and mediates nociception: released by enteroendocrine cells on distension; it is also the pain signal from a stretched gut.
  • Gastrin = stimulates gastric acid: from G cells, acting on parietal and ECL cells via CCK2 receptors.
  • Somatostatin = inhibits gastric acid: from D cells when pH falls below 3.

stem: Match the type of contraction with its corresponding function in the large intestine.

items.left: Tonic contraction of the ileocecal valve
items.right: Prevents bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine

items.left: Tonic contraction of the external anal sphincter
items.right: Allows for the voluntary control of the defecation reflex
Sustained peristaltic contraction that facilitates the excretion of feces

answer:
The pairings:

Type of contractionFunction
Haustral contractionAbsorption of water and electrolytes
Tonic contraction of the ileocecal valvePrevents bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine
Tonic contraction of the external anal sphincterAllows for the voluntary control of the defecation reflex
Mass movementSustained peristaltic contraction that facilitates the excretion of feces

From 02 - Gastrointestinal Motility. Each colonic contraction pattern has one job:

  • Haustral contraction = absorption of water and electrolytes: a segmentation-type squeeze of the waste bolus, mainly in the ascending colon, that wrings out water.
  • Tonic contraction of the ileocecal valve = preventing bacterial overgrowth in the small intestine: like every sphincter it is tonically closed, stopping bacteria-laden colonic contents refluxing into the relatively sterile ileum.
  • Tonic contraction of the external anal sphincter = voluntary control of defecation: it is striated muscle, so relaxing it is a learned, voluntary act.
  • Mass movement = sustained peristalsis that expels feces: 1-3 large pushes a day toward the rectum, triggered by the gastrocolic reflex after a meal.
note: answer key A-i, B-iii, C-iv, D-ii

stem: Match the correct embryological gut tube structure with its blood supply:
answer:
The pairings:

Gut tube divisionBlood supply
ForegutCeliac trunk
MidgutSuperior mesenteric artery
HindgutInferior mesenteric artery

From 05 - Development of the GI Tract. Each division of the gut tube carries its own artery through the dorsal mesentery:

  • Celiac trunk = foregut: esophagus to the proximal duodenum, plus the liver, gallbladder and pancreas.
  • SMA = midgut: distal duodenum to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon. The midgut loop rotates around the SMA during physiologic herniation.
  • IMA = hindgut: distal third of the transverse colon to the upper anal canal. Its superior rectal branch supplies the rectum.

This matters clinically: the appendix (midgut) refers pain to the umbilicus, and the sigmoid (hindgut) refers it suprapubically.
note: answer key A-i, B-iii, C-ii

stem: Match the fully developed structure with the embryological structure it developed from
answer:
The pairings:

Developed structureEmbryological origin
DuodenumForegut tube
Greater omentumDorsal mesentery
Hepatogastric ligamentVentral mesentery
StomachForegut tube
PancreasForegut tube
Bile ductForegut tube
LiverForegut tube
Falciform ligamentVentral mesentery
Hepatoduodenal ligamentVentral mesentery
GallbladderForegut tube

From 05 - Development of the GI Tract. Sort each structure by what it grows from:

  • Foregut tube: the organs themselves. The duodenum (the first part is foregut), stomach, pancreas (dorsal and ventral buds off the duodenal endoderm), bile duct, liver and gallbladder, which all come from the hepatic diverticulum.
  • Ventral mesentery: the liver grows into it, and it splits into the falciform ligament anterior to the liver and the lesser omentum behind it, which comprises the hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments.
  • Dorsal mesentery: as the stomach rotates it elongates, folds down four layers thick and fuses into the greater omentum.

The trap is the liver: it develops within the ventral mesentery, but it is a foregut outgrowth, not the mesentery itself.

stem: Match the structure with the correct fold that it lies within on the internal aspect of the anterior abdominal wall.
answer:
The pairings:

StructureFold
Obliterated umbilical arteryMedial umbilical fold
Inferior epigastric vesselsLateral umbilical fold
Obliterated urachusMedian umbilical fold

All of these structures head superiorly towards the umbilicus. The only functioning structure is the inferior epigastric vessels found within the lateral umbilical fold. These vessels course superiorly to anastomose with the superior epigastric vessels. The other two structures are embryological remnants. In the direct midline, the umbilical ligament (obliterated urachus) forms the median umbilical fold. The urachus, was the developmental connection from the bladder to the umbilicus in the fetus, which was originally developed from the allantois. The obliterated umbilical arteries create the medial umbilical fold, and when they were patent, during development, they carried deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta.
note: answer key A-ii, B-iii, C-i

answer:
The pairings:

FeatureStructure
Thick interrupted mucosal foldsColon
Often contain fecal materialColon
Normal diameter <3 cmSmall bowel
Located centrally within the abdomenSmall bowel

From 07 - GI Imaging. The lecture's small-versus-large-bowel table has four discriminators on plain film:

  • Small bowel: sits centrally, with a normal diameter under 3 cm. Its folds, the plicae circulares, are continuous and cross the whole lumen, and it rarely contains feces.
  • Colon: forms a peripheral picture frame. Its folds are the thick, interrupted haustra that do not span the lumen, it usually contains fecal material, and it runs up to 6 cm, or 9 cm at the cecum.

Learn the numbers as a 3-6-9 rule: small bowel 3, colon 6, cecum 9.

stem: Match the potential side effect of antihistamines with the type receptor most likely associated with it.
answer:
The pairings:

Side effectReceptor
Postural hypotensionAntagonism of alpha-adrenergic receptors
SedationAntagonism of H1 receptors
Dry mouthAntagonism of muscarinic receptors
Weight gainAntagonism of serotonin receptors

From 08 - PUD, Dyspepsia, & Acid-Lowering Drugs (the antiemetic chart). First-generation antihistamines cross the blood-brain barrier and bind receptors beyond H1. Each off-target receptor explains one side effect:

  • Postural hypotension = alpha-adrenergic blockade: loss of the vasoconstriction that supports standing blood pressure, which also causes dizziness.
  • Sedation = central H1 blockade: the on-target effect in the brain, which is why patients are warned about combining it with benzodiazepines.
  • Dry mouth = muscarinic blockade, alongside urinary retention and sinus tachycardia.
  • Weight gain = serotonin blockade, through increased appetite.
note: answer key i-B, ii-A, iii-D, iv-C

stem: Match each of the following to either ALT > AST or AST > ALT.
answer:
The pairings:

ConditionEnzyme pattern
NAFLDALT > AST
Acute Budd-Chiari syndromeAST > ALT
Alcoholic liver diseaseAST > ALT
Viral hepatitisALT > AST
Celiac diseaseALT > AST
Ischemic hepatitisAST > ALT

From 03 - Approach to Abnormal Liver Enzymes. AST is found outside the liver (muscle, red cells, brain) and falls in mitochondria-heavy, alcoholic, ischemic or vascular injury; ALT is the more liver-specific enzyme and dominates in most inflammatory or metabolic hepatocellular injury. The lecture's lists sort each item:

  • NAFLD = ALT > AST: steatosis and NASH are ALT-predominant.
  • Acute Budd-Chiari = AST > ALT: hepatic venous outflow obstruction behaves like ischemic or congestive injury.
  • Alcoholic liver disease = AST > ALT: classically at 2:1 or more.
  • Viral hepatitis = ALT > AST: acute or chronic.
  • Celiac disease = ALT > AST: a systemic cause of mild ALT elevation.
  • Ischemic hepatitis = AST > ALT, grouped with congestive hepatopathy.
